daifExplainer.explainerParagraph: The term <1>ḍaʿīf</1> means the chain of transmission has a flaw — a narrator with weak memory, an unknown link, or a break — so the words cannot be attributed to the Prophet ﷺ with confidence. It does not automatically mean the meaning is false. Many scholars permit acting on a weak report to encourage good deeds (faḍāʾil al-aʿmāl) provided nothing is treated as an established ruling or a guaranteed reward; others decline to use them at all. prayerTimes.awwabinHadith: "Whoever prays six rak'ahs after Maghrib without speaking anything bad between them, those six rak'ahs will be counted for him as equivalent to twelve years of worship." — Sunan Ibn Majah 1167; Abu Hurayrah (RA): "My close friend advised me to pray two rak'ahs of Duha and not to sleep before praying Witr." — Sahih al-Bukhari 1981

prayerTimes.forbiddenSunriseNote: Prayer is not allowed from sunrise until ~20 min after the sun has fully cleared the horizon.
prayerTimes.forbiddenSunsetHadith: "At three times the Prophet ﷺ forbade us to pray: ... when it is about to set." — Sahih Muslim 831; Sahih al-Bukhari 586
prayerTimes.forbiddenSunsetNote: Prayer is forbidden during the ~17 minutes the sun visibly sets (turns yellow and descends to the horizon). This is the "time of sunset" mentioned in the hadith. Nafl is allowed between Asr and this window. Obligatory (qada) make-up prayers are permitted. Maghrib begins shortly after sunset.
prayerTimes.forbiddenZenithHadith: "At three times the Prophet ﷺ forbade us to pray ... when it is at its zenith." — Sahih Muslim 831; Ibn 'Umar: "Do not pray when the sun is rising, nor when it is setting, nor when it is at its peak (zenith)." — Sahih al-Bukhari 585
prayerTimes.forbiddenZenithNote: The sun is directly overhead (~10 min before Dhuhr). Prayer is forbidden until Dhuhr time begins.

prayerTimes.ishraqDuhaHadith: "Whoever prays Fajr in congregation, then sits remembering Allah until the sun rises, then prays two rak'ahs — he will have a reward like that of Hajj and 'Umrah, complete, complete, complete." — Tirmidhi 586; Duha: "The Prophet ﷺ used to pray Duha four rak'ahs and would add more as Allah willed." — Sahih Muslim 717
prayerTimes.ishraqDuhaNote: 2–8 voluntary rak'ahs. Best time is when the sun has risen well (Ishraq = 20 min after sunrise). Duha can continue until just before the solar zenith. Immense reward equivalent to Hajj and 'Umrah.

privacy.seoDescription: How Bustandeen stores and protects your data: what we collect, what stays on your device, what friends can see, how the optional AI works, and your control over deletion.
privacy.contactText: Have a question or concern about your privacy? We'd love to help.
privacy.heading: Privacy
privacy.subtitle: Short, honest, no legalese.

whatWeStore.title: What we store
whatWeStore.body0: Your email and sign-in details (from Firebase, using email or Google), a display name, and a profile photo and country if you add them. We never store your password.
whatWeStore.body1: Worship logs: zikr counts, salat statuses (including home or mosque, and your kaza ledger), fasting, Quran progress, hifz progress and Ramadan data. These are tied to your user ID, never to your device fingerprint.
whatWeStore.body2: Timing details: when you count zikr (kept for 90 days, to power session history and the time-of-day chart) and when you read or listen to the Quran (start, end and active minutes of each session).
whatWeStore.body3: Rayhanah Cycle data, if you use it: start and end dates, daily flow, symptom and mood notes, and the height and weight you choose to add. Notes and body stats are encrypted (AES-256-GCM) before they reach the database.
whatWeStore.body4: Friends: mutual connections, and the Noor scores worked out from your own activity.
whatWeStore.body5: Messages you send us: feedback and contact forms, zikr requests, and sadaqah donation details (optional name, email, phone, payment method, transaction ID, amount, date, message, and an IP address to prevent abuse).
whatWeStore.body6: The time you were last active, and the service emails we send: a welcome, replies to your messages, donation status, and occasionally a gentle note after a long break.

deviceOnly.title: Stays on your device only
deviceOnly.body0: Your prayer-times location (latitude and longitude). It is used to calculate times on your device and is never sent to our servers.
deviceOnly.body1: If you search for a city by name, the search text goes to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service to find its coordinates.
deviceOnly.body2: Preferences (language, units, discreet mode, hide BMI), cached Quran text, counts waiting to sync while you are offline, and your sign-in token.

friendsSee.title: What friends can see
friendsSee.body0: Only confirmed friends see your row: display name, photo, country flag, and your Noor (today and this week).
friendsSee.body1: A few small chips: prayers done today, zikr streak, today's zikr count, whether you are fasting, and Quran āyāt against your goal. Never times, notes, places, or which dhikr you did.
friendsSee.body2: You can hide from every friend's leaderboard at any time with the invisible setting in Friends.
friendsSee.body3: Rayhanah data is never visible to friends. On your excused days the numbers are filled from what you actually did, so nothing reveals it.
friendsSee.body4: The one exception is opt-in: if you choose to share your cycle status with a friend, she sees only a yes or no (never a date, symptom or note), and her view of your row hides the prayer and fasting chips. You can turn this off at any moment.

naseeh.title: Naseeh (optional AI)
naseeh.body0: Naseeh is off unless you turn it on in Settings. It uses an AI service (Groq) to phrase encouragement, weekly reflections, and to read the sentence you type in quick log.
naseeh.body1: What is sent: short summaries such as counts, streaks and percentages, and the sentence you type into quick log. Your name, email, Rayhanah notes, dates and body stats are never sent.
naseeh.body2: Two Rayhanah touches, only when Naseeh is on: the gentle comfort line may send the mood or symptom words you chose that day, and cycle guidance sends only the phase and day number.
naseeh.body3: We do not use your data to train any model, and Naseeh gives encouragement, never religious rulings. You can use your own Groq key (stored encrypted) and turn Naseeh off at any time.

thirdParty.title: Services we rely on
thirdParty.body0: Google Analytics 4 counts page views and anonymous usage patterns (with IP anonymised). No worship data is ever sent to it.
thirdParty.body1: Firebase (Google) handles sign-in, Vercel hosts the app, and MongoDB Atlas stores the database.
thirdParty.body2: Quran text, tafsir and recitation audio come from quran.com, alquran.cloud, the Islamic Network and mp3quran; flags come from flagcdn and fonts from Google Fonts. Like any website, those services can see your IP address when your device loads their files.

neverDo.title: What we never do
neverDo.body0: Sell, share, or monetise your data. There are no ads, no trackers beyond Google Analytics, and no affiliate links.
neverDo.body1: Store passwords. Sign-in is handled entirely by Firebase (Google).
neverDo.body2: Show your worship details to anyone, or turn your dīn into a competition where a quiet day is shamed. Noor is only ever encouragement.

yourControl.title: Your control
yourControl.body0: Export everything as a JSON backup or Excel file from Settings.
yourControl.body1: Delete any feature's data separately from the Settings danger zone.
yourControl.body2: Delete your entire account and all server-side data from your Profile page.
yourControl.body3: Go invisible to friends, turn Naseeh off, remove your saved height and weight, or use discreet mode, each with a tap.

protected.title: How it's protected
protected.body0: All data in transit is encrypted (HTTPS/TLS).
protected.body1: Access is restricted by Firebase Auth tokens, so only your own requests can read or write your data.
protected.body2: Rayhanah notes, body stats and your own AI key are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM before they are stored.
protected.body3: The server runs on Vercel's infrastructure (SOC 2 Type II compliant), with the database on MongoDB Atlas.

info.byWeekdayBody: Your completion rate for each day of the week, added up across the whole period you're viewing — not a timeline. It answers "which day am I weakest on," e.g. Friday afternoons or Monday Fajr. A day with no bar yet just has no data in this window.
info.prayerTimingBody: Of the prayers you've marked done, how far into that prayer's valid time window you tended to pray it — early, mid, or late. Only counts prayers where your location was set at the time (the window itself is calculated from prayer times, which need a location).
info.kazaDebtChartBody: How many missed prayers you added to your kaza debt (red) vs paid back by completing a make-up prayer (green), grouped by day for a short window, or into up to 12 equal bars (weekly, wider for a year or all time) that together cover the whole period. The rightmost bar always ends on the last day of the period, and hovering any bar shows its exact date range.
info.correlationBody: Compares how often you catch Fajr on time the morning after praying Isha before 11pm vs after 11pm — a purely personal pattern from your own last 90 days, not a religious ruling. It only appears once there's enough data in BOTH categories (at least 5 days each) — a 2-day sample would just be noise dressed up as a percentage.
info.mosqueTrendBody: What share of your prayers were prayed at the mosque (in jama’ah), tracked day by day for a short window, or in up to 12 equal steps (weekly, wider for a year or all time) that together cover the whole period. The rightmost point ends on the last day of the period, and its label shows the exact date range it covers.
info.prayerCalendarBody: Every day in the window, colored by how many of your 5 daily prayers were completed that day — from red (0) to bright green (all 5). Today is ringed in green. A faint, near-invisible cell means no data at all for that day (nothing logged, or it hasn't happened yet), which is different from a red cell (logged, but nothing done).
info.journeyBody: Your tracking history split into phases — a new phase starts each time you reset your kaza debt count. Each phase shows how many days it covered and your completion rate across them. The current (ongoing) phase's numbers update live and already include today's progress so far.
info.kazaInsightsBody: A closer look at your makeup prayer patterns — which missed prayers you've been carrying longest, how quickly you typically pay them back, and which prayer tends to linger. Only counts prayers the tracker knows an exact missed date for.

settings.dayStartFajrInfoBody:
Your tracking day begins the moment Fajr (dawn) starts at your saved location — not at midnight. So if you pray Isha late, or have suhoor before dawn, that still counts toward the day that's ending, not the new one, matching how a worship day actually flows.

This needs your saved prayer location to calculate Fajr's exact time (Settings → Prayer times location, using the same calculation method as your Prayer Times page). Without a location, it quietly falls back to plain midnight until you add one.

Example: if Fajr is at 4:12 AM and you pray Isha at 1:00 AM, that Isha — and everything before 4:12 AM — still belongs to yesterday's tracking day.
settings.dayStartMidnightInfoBody:
Your tracking day flips at exactly 12:00 AM local time — the plain calendar-day boundary your phone's clock already uses. This is also what Fasting already tracks by, regardless of which option you pick here.

No location needed — this works immediately on any device.

Example: if you pray Isha at 1:00 AM, that already counts as a brand-new day the moment the clock struck midnight, even though you haven't slept yet.
settings.dayStartMaghribInfoBody:
Follows the Islamic calendar's own day boundary: a new Hijri day begins at Maghrib (sunset), not at midnight — the same way the Hijri date shown elsewhere in the app already changes at sunset, not midnight.

Like Fajr-to-Fajr, this needs your saved prayer location to calculate Maghrib's exact time. Without one, it falls back to plain midnight too.

Example: if Maghrib is at 6:30 PM on Tuesday, everything from 6:30 PM Tuesday through 6:29 PM Wednesday belongs to the same tracking day — matching how the Hijri date itself already works.
settings.dayStartInfoAppliesTo: Applies to your Zikr counter, Salat tracker and Quran reading — their daily reset, streaks and "today" all follow whichever option you pick. Fasting and your salat kaza-debt history always use the plain calendar date no matter what, since a fast is dawn-to-sunset of one fixed date.

arafah.name: Day of Arafah

0.text: "Fasting the Day of Arafah expiates the sins of the previous and coming year." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1162

1.text: "The best du'ā is du'ā on the Day of Arafah." — Tirmidhī 3585

2.text: "Today I have perfected your religion for you..." — Quran 5:3

arafah.shortDesc: 9th Dhul Ḥijjah — the best day of the year. Fasting expiates two years of sins.
arafah.significance: The Day of Arafah is the best day in the whole year. On this day, millions of pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah in the greatest act of worship. For those not on Ḥajj, the Prophet ﷺ strongly recommended fasting — it expiates the sins of the previous year and the coming year. Allah descends and boasts to His angels about the people of Arafah. This is also the day Islam was perfected.

0.action: Fast the Day of Arafah (9th Dhul Ḥijjah)
0.note: Expiates two years of sins — do not miss it!

1.action: Spend the day in du'ā, dhikr, and Quran
1.note: Best du'ā: "Lā ilāha illAllāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lahu, lahu l-mulku wa lahu l-ḥamdu wa huwa 'alā kulli shay'in qadīr"

3.action: Give ṣadaqah and increase in righteous deeds

ashura.name: 'Āshūrā

0.text: "Fasting the day of 'Āshūrā expiates the sins of the previous year." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1162

1.text: "If I live until next year, I will fast the 9th as well." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1134

ashura.shortDesc: 10th Muharram — fasting expiates the previous year's sins. Also fast the 9th.
ashura.significance: The Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina and found the Jews fasting on this day. They told him it was the day Allah saved Musa (Moses) ﷺ and drowned Pharaoh. The Prophet ﷺ said 'We have more right to Musa than you do' and fasted and commanded fasting. He intended to also fast the 9th to differ from the People of the Book. Fasting 'Āshūrā expiates the sins of the previous year.

0.note: To differ from the People of the Book — the Prophet intended to do this

3.action: Reflect on the story of Musa ﷺ — Allah's deliverance of the believers

ayyam_al_bid.name: Ayyām al-Bīḍ

0.text: "Fast three days of every month — the 13th, 14th, and 15th." — Sunan Abū Dāwūd 2449

1.text: "Fasting three days of every month is like fasting the whole year." — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1979

ayyam_al_bid.shortDesc: 13th, 14th, 15th of every Islamic month — fasting equivalent to fasting the whole month.
ayyam_al_bid.significance: The Prophet ﷺ never abandoned fasting the three white days — the 13th, 14th, and 15th of each Islamic month. These are called 'the white days' because the full moon illuminates the night. Fasting these three days is like fasting the entire month, for each good deed is multiplied ten times.

0.note: Equivalent to fasting the whole month

1.action: Observe the full moon — reflect on Allah's creation

2.action: Increase Quran recitation in these blessed nights

dhul_hijjah_first10.name: First 10 Days of Dhul Ḥijjah

0.text: "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these ten days." — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 969

1.text: By the dawn; and the ten nights (89:1-2) — these are the ten days of Dhul Ḥijjah, per Ibn 'Abbās (RA)

dhul_hijjah_first10.shortDesc: The greatest days for good deeds — outweigh even jihād in virtue.
dhul_hijjah_first10.significance: These are the ten days Allah swore by in the Quran (89:2). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these ten days.' Good deeds in these days — including fasting, dhikr (especially tahlīl, takbīr, taḥmīd), Quran recitation, ṣadaqah, and qiyām — are multiplied and more beloved to Allah than even those done in other times.

0.action: Increase tahlīl (Lā ilāha illallāh), takbīr (Allāhu Akbar), taḥmīd (Alḥamdulillāh), and tasbīḥ (SubḥānAllāh)

1.action: Fast the first 9 days if able (especially Day of Arafah — 9th)

2.action: Give ṣadaqah generously throughout these 10 days

3.action: Increase Quran recitation and complete a khatm if possible

4.action: Perform extra nawāfil prayers — especially Tahajjud

5.action: If planning Qurbānī — do not cut hair or nails from 1st Dhul Ḥijjah

eid_adha.name: Eid al-Aḍḥā
eid_adha.shortDesc: 10th Dhul Ḥijjah — the greater Eid. Eid prayer, Qurbānī, and celebration.
eid_adha.significance: Eid al-Aḍḥā is the greater Eid, coinciding with the Day of Naḥr (sacrifice) when Ḥājjīs perform their sacrifice after the Day of Arafah. Muslims worldwide offer Qurbānī (an animal sacrifice) to commemorate the sacrifice of Ibrāhīm ﷺ. It is a day of gratitude, prayer, and celebration. Fasting on this day is ḥarām.

1.note: Wājib (Ḥanafī) or Sunnah Muakkadah (other madhāhib) for those who are able

2.action: Recite takbīr al-Tashrīq from Fajr of 9th to Asr of 13th Dhul Ḥijjah

3.action: Distribute Qurbānī meat: 1/3 family, 1/3 neighbours, 1/3 poor

4.action: Do NOT fast today — fasting is ḥarām on Eid al-Aḍḥā

eid_fitr.name: Eid al-Fiṭr

0.text: Eid prayer and its rulings — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 950

1.text: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would eat an odd number of dates before going out on the morning of Eid al-Fiṭr." — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 953

eid_fitr.shortDesc: 1st Shawwāl — celebrate the completion of Ramadan. Eid prayer is wājib.
eid_fitr.significance: Eid al-Fiṭr marks the end of Ramadan and is a day of pure joy and gratitude. Fasting on this day is forbidden (ḥarām). The Eid prayer is wājib (required by many scholars) or Sunnah Muakkadah. Muslims pay Zakāt al-Fiṭr before the prayer, exchange Eid greetings, visit family, and celebrate Allah's blessing of completing Ramadan.

0.note: Wājib/Sunnah Muakkadah — do not miss it

1.action: Pay Zakāt al-Fiṭr before the Eid prayer
1.note: Must be paid before prayer to count — a grain-based charity

2.action: Eat something sweet (dates) before Eid prayer
2.note: Sunnah — the Prophet ﷺ ate an odd number of dates before going out

3.action: Recite takbīr until the Eid prayer begins
3.note: Allāhu Akbar, Allāhu Akbar, Lā ilāha illAllāhu, Allāhu Akbar, Allāhu Akbar wa lillāhil ḥamd

4.action: Visit family, exchange gifts, spread joy

5.action: Do NOT fast today — fasting is ḥarām on Eid al-Fiṭr

fast_mon_thu.name: Sunnah Fast Day

0.text: "Those are two days on which deeds are presented to the Lord of the Worlds, and I like for my deeds to be presented when I am fasting." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1162

1.text: "The du'ā of a fasting person at the time of breaking fast is not rejected." — Sunan Ibn Mājah 1753

fast_mon_thu.shortDesc: Monday & Thursday — the Prophet ﷺ fasted these days. Deeds are presented to Allah.
fast_mon_thu.significance: The Prophet ﷺ was asked about fasting on Monday and Thursday. He said: 'Those are two days on which people's deeds are presented to the Lord of the Worlds and I would like my deeds to be presented when I am fasting.' Fasting Monday and Thursday is among the most regularly observed sunnah fasts.

0.action: Make intention (niyyah) for fasting before Fajr
0.note: Or you may intend in the morning if you have not eaten

2.action: Increase dhikr and istighfār throughout the fasting hours

3.action: Make du'ā at iftār — the fasting person's du'ā is not rejected

specialDays.footerQuote: "Whoever acts on knowledge given to him, Allah will give him knowledge of what he did not know." — Ibn al-Qayyim

friday.name: Friday — Jumu'ah

0.text: "The best day the sun rises upon is Friday." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 854

2.text: "Whoever reads Surah Al-Kahf on Friday will be illuminated between the two Fridays." — al-Mustadrak 2/399

3.text: "On Friday there is a time in which a Muslim does not ask Allah for anything but He gives it to him." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 852

4.text: "Send abundant ṣalawāt on me on Fridays — for your ṣalawāt is presented to me." — Sunan Abū Dāwūd 1047

friday.shortDesc: The master of days. Attend Jumu'ah, read Surah Al-Kahf, send abundant ṣalawāt.
friday.significance: Friday is the best day the sun rises upon. Allah made it a day of gathering (Jumu'ah), supplication, ṣalawāt on the Prophet ﷺ, and the reading of Surah Al-Kahf. There is a hidden hour on Friday in which any du'ā is accepted. The Jumu'ah prayer (khutbah + 2 rak'ahs in congregation) replaces Dhuhr for adult Muslim men.

1.action: Attend Jumu'ah prayer in congregation at a mosque
1.note: Farḍ — obligatory for adult Muslim men

2.note: Illuminates with light from Friday to Friday

3.action: Send abundant ṣalawāt on the Prophet ﷺ

4.action: Make du'ā between Asr and Maghrib
4.note: The hidden hour of acceptance — do not miss it

5.action: Increase dhikr, istighfār, and Quran recitation throughout the day

6.action: Cut nails, wear best clothes, use miswāk and fragrance

islamic_new_year.name: Islamic New Year

0.text: "The best fasting after Ramadan is fasting in the month of Muḥarram." — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1163

islamic_new_year.shortDesc: 1st Muḥarram — the Hijrī year begins. Reflect on the Prophet ﷺ's migration.
islamic_new_year.significance: The Islamic New Year marks the beginning of the Hijrī calendar, established after the migration (Hijra) of the Prophet ﷺ from Mecca to Medina. Muḥarram is one of the four sacred months in Islam. It is a time for reflection, renewed intentions, and increased worship. The Quran mentions: 'Allah's count of months is twelve' (9:36). There is no specific act of worship legislated for this day — it is a time for reflection.

0.action: Reflect on the Hijra and its lessons of sacrifice and trust in Allah

1.action: Renew your intention (niyyah) for the year ahead

2.action: Increase worship in this sacred month of Muḥarram

laylat_qadr.name: Laylat al-Qadr

0.text: "Laylat al-Qadr is better than a thousand months." — Quran 97:3

1.text: "Seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan." — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2017

2.text: The Laylat al-Qadr du'ā — Sunan al-Tirmidhī 3513

laylat_qadr.shortDesc: Odd nights of the last 10 of Ramadan — better than 1000 months of worship.
laylat_qadr.significance: Laylat al-Qadr is the night the Quran was revealed and the greatest night of the year. Worship on this single night is better than 83+ years of worship. The Prophet ﷺ would seclude himself (i'tikāf) in the last 10 nights of Ramadan and seek it especially on odd nights. The signs include a calm, temperate night and the sun rising with no rays the next morning.

0.action: Pray Tarāwīḥ/Qiyām al-Layl throughout the night

1.action: Recite the du'ā: 'Allāhumma innaka 'afuwwun tuḥibb al-'afwa fa'fu 'annī'
1.note: "O Allah, You are Most Forgiving and love forgiveness, so forgive me." — Tirmidhī 3513

2.action: Recite the Quran extensively throughout the night

3.action: Make abundant istighfār, ṣalawāt, and dhikr

4.action: Give ṣadaqah — multiplied infinitely on this night

5.action: Pray Fajr in congregation — completing the night

shab_e_barat.name: Laylat al-Barā'ah

0.text: "Allah looks down on the night of the 15th of Sha'bān and forgives all His creation except a mushrik or a spiteful person." — Sunan Ibn Mājah 1389

1.text: Scholarly discussion on Sha'bān 15 — see Ibn Rajab's Laṭā'if al-Ma'ārif

shab_e_barat.shortDesc: 15th Sha'bān night — Allah forgives abundantly. Some scholars consider this established.
shab_e_barat.significance: On the night of the 15th of Sha'bān (i.e., the night between 14th and 15th), some hadith reports indicate that Allah looks upon His creation and forgives all except those who associate partners with Him and those who harbour enmity. Many scholars (including Imam Ahmad, Ibn Rajab, and al-Albānī) consider this night to have virtue. However, there is scholarly disagreement — the reports are weak by some standards but ḥasan by others. Observe this night with worship if you believe in its virtue, but don't innovate specific rituals with no established basis.

0.action: Spend the night in qiyām, du'ā, and dhikr

1.note: Many scholars recommend fasting this day

3.action: Recite Quran and reflect on your life

prohibitedDetail.eid_fitr: Fasting on the day of Eid al-Fiṭr is ḥarām — it is the day Allah commanded us to break the fast and celebrate.
prohibitedDetail.eid_adha: Fasting on the day of sacrifice is ḥarām — it is a day of eating from the qurbānī and celebration.
prohibitedDetail.tashriq: The three days after Eid al-Aḍḥā are days of eating, drinking, and remembering Allah — fasting them is prohibited (exception: a pilgrim without a sacrificial animal).

dislikedDetail.friday_alone: Do not fast Friday by itself — join it with Thursday or Saturday. (Fine when it coincides with a habit or a specific day like ʿArafah.)
dislikedDetail.saturday_alone: Singling out Saturday for voluntary fasting is discouraged by some scholars (it is the day the Jews venerate). Joined with Friday or Sunday, or coinciding with ʿArafah/ʿĀshūrā, it is fine. There is scholarly difference on this hadith.
dislikedDetail.day_of_doubt: Fasting the day when Ramadan's start is uncertain is prohibited by most scholars — unless it matches a fasting habit you already keep (e.g. it falls on your usual Monday fast).
dislikedDetail.wisal: Fasting day and night continuously without breaking is forbidden — the Prophet ﷺ said no one is like him in this.
